Subject: Moving Arvind to the quality role

Hi Trisha,

It has been six weeks since Arvind's improvement plan started. On backend tasks, four of nine are done and the rest needed rework. On testing, Arvind found eleven bugs we had missed and wrote a checklist the whole team now uses. I don't think Arvind is failing. I think we put him in the wrong seat. Could we move him to the quality role from the next sprint? I would keep the same daily check-ins and the same review date. I'd like your agreement before I tell him, so that he hears one clear message.

Thanks,
Rafiq

qa.q: How many bugs did Arvind find that the team had missed?
qa.a: Arvind found eleven bugs the team had missed.

qa.q: What does Rafiq think about Arvind's progress?
qa.a: Rafiq sees a mismatch rather than a failure, and feels concerned but hopeful that a different role will suit Arvind.

qa.q: What else could Rafiq do when telling Arvind, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq could explain what Arvind did well in testing and what the new role will ask for, because the move then feels like recognition rather than demotion.

qa.q: How might Trisha see this request?
qa.a: Trisha probably sees a lead who looked at facts and thought about the person's strengths, which makes it easier to agree.

grounding: Illustrates moving a junior with patchy backend progress but strong testing into a quality role that suits his strengths, with the manager's agreement.

passage:
Trisha, you asked me for a story where a plan didn't work out the way I expected. Here's one.
Last year I had a junior, Sunil, struggling on backend work. I'm Pankaj, I lead the platform team, and I did everything by the book: a six-week plan, goals, weekly check-ins.
At the six-week review, the backend goals were patchy. One done, two half done. But I noticed something in my notes. Every week, the thing he did best was testing. He'd found bugs nobody else caught. He wrote test cases like he enjoyed it.
So I asked myself, am I trying to fix the wrong thing? I spoke to my manager, and she agreed to try him in the QA team.
Three months later he's the one people ask when a release looks risky. That plan failing was the best thing that happened.

qa.q: How many of the backend goals were fully done at the six-week review?
How might Sunil have felt doing testing work, according to Pankaj?
qa.a: Pankaj says Sunil wrote test cases like he enjoyed them, which suggests Sunil felt more engaged and confident in testing than in backend work.

qa.q: What was the key signal Pankaj noticed, and what did it change?
qa.a: Pankaj noticed from the notes that testing was Sunil's strongest work every week, which changed the plan from fixing backend skills to moving him to a quality role.

qa.q: How did the move look to Pankaj's manager?
qa.a: The manager agreed to try it, likely seeing a sensible way to keep a capable person in a role that matched his strengths.

grounding: It shows a lead noticing after six weeks that progress was patchy on backend but strong in testing, and with the manager's agreement moving him to a quality role.

I sit across from Eshaan's desk, so I watched this over a couple of months.
Eshaan had put Kunwar, our newest developer, on a six-week plan for the backend work. Every Friday they met. I'd hear bits of it: "the API is still failing," "this one's better."
Around week six I saw Eshaan staring at the whiteboard for a long time. He'd written two columns: "backend: patchy" and "testing: strong." Kunwar's test reports had been the best on the team for weeks. People had started forwarding them.
The next Monday, Eshaan went into our manager's office for half an hour. That afternoon, it was announced that Kunwar would move to the quality team.
I can't say what Eshaan was thinking at the whiteboard. But I saw Kunwar walk out of that meeting with his shoulders lighter than I'd seen in weeks. — Vinita

qa.q: What were the two columns Eshaan wrote on the whiteboard?
What does Eshaan staring at the whiteboard for a long time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was thoughtful and perhaps uneasy, weighing whether the plan was fixing the wrong thing before changing course.

qa.q: What else could Eshaan have done if the manager had said no to the move?
qa.a: He could have kept Kunwar on backend but added testing tasks and support, adjusting the goals to build on his strengths.

qa.q: How did the change look to Kunwar, as far as the observer could tell?
qa.a: Kunwar seemed relieved; he walked out of the meeting with lighter shoulders, suggesting the new role felt like a better fit.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, a lead seeing patchy backend progress but strong testing after six weeks and moving the junior to a quality role with the manager's agreement.
